h1:
Phang Nga Food Guide
Seafood, Hokkien Noodles & Southern Thai
intro: Phang Nga is a better eating destination than most visitors expect. The Takua Pa side has Hokkien-style breakfasts passed down through generations. The town centre and piers pull in fresh seafood from Phang Nga Bay daily. And fiery Southern Thai food is on the menu across the entire province. We put together local-verified picks — useful whether you are stopping through on the way to Khao Lak or heading out to the bay.

blocks.html: Phang Nga's food scene is a genuinely interesting mix. The Hokkien Chinese community that settled here during the tin-mining era left a clear stamp on the breakfast table around Takua Pa — Hokkien mee, hor mok, and dim sum you can still find at decades-old shophouses. Meanwhile the sea on both sides of the province keeps the seafood fresh and the prices honest. We split the food into three main categories, then followed up with specific shops locals recommend.

If you had to pick one dish that defines Phang Nga for locals, most would say Hokkien mee — thick yellow noodles stir-fried in a rich sauce with pork, shrimp, and fish balls, often finished with a soft-set egg on top. You eat it with fresh bean sprouts, cucumber, shallots, and a squeeze of lime. The old market area of Takua Pa is where you will find this done the way it has always been done.

items.name: Hokkien Mee
items.blurb: Thick yellow noodles stir-fried in a sticky, fragrant sauce — chewy, savoury, topped with a soft egg. Served with fresh veg on the side. This is the dish that comes to mind first when people think of eating in Takua Pa.

items.name: Hokkien Hor Mok
items.blurb: A steamed fish curry cake with roots in the old Tai Mueang mining community, made fresh daily. Some shops also offer it as a steamed bun filling or deep-fried — worth trying all three formats.

items.name: Takua Pa Dim Sum
items.blurb: Morning dim sum the way Southern Thai-Chinese families do it — har gow, siu mai, bao — alongside old-school kopitiam coffee. Old market shops open before dawn and usually sell out well before noon.

items.name: Oh Aew
items.blurb: A Hokkien-heritage cold dessert made from banana seed jelly and grass jelly, sweetened and served over shaved ice. Exactly what you need to cool down after a plate of fiery Southern curry.

blocks.title: Timing tip
blocks.html: Most breakfast and dim sum shops in the Takua Pa old market open early and close before noon — some shut on Mondays. If you are targeting a popular spot, check their opening day and aim to arrive before 10 am to be safe.

Phang Nga is flanked by the bay on one side and the Andaman Sea near Khao Lak on the other, so seafood is genuinely fresh and noticeably cheaper here than in bigger tourist towns. Order shrimp, crab, shellfish, or local fish cooked Southern-style. If you are after value, look for restaurants that offer set meals per person. If atmosphere matters, there are waterfront and sea-view places scattered across several neighbourhoods.

items: Tamarind shrimp — Prawns fried and tossed in a tangy-sweet tamarind sauce. A staple at seafood restaurants around Koh Kloy and Tha Nun, near Sarasin Bridge.
Stir-fried crab & local shellfish — Blue swimmer or mud crab stir-fried with curry powder or black pepper, alongside seasonal shellfish straight from the bay.
Per-person set meals — Some restaurants around Bang Phat offer set menus at around ฿250/person with multiple dishes to share — good value for groups.

blocks.title: Ordering seafood smart
blocks.html: Always ask the price per kilogram and the weight before you order — especially for shrimp and crab, which fluctuate with the season. Local restaurants are usually upfront about this, so do not hesitate to ask.

Southern Thai cooking in Phang Nga is serious about spice and aromatics. If you can handle the heat, this is paradise. If you are not used to very spicy food, just tell the kitchen — most places will dial it back. The menu runs from intensely spiced dishes like gaeng tai pla all the way to gentler crowd-pleasers like moo hong.

items.name: Grilled Shrimp Paste Relish (Nam Prik Kung Siab)
items.blurb: A Southern-style nam prik built around grilled dried shrimp paste, served with fresh and blanched vegetables. Found on nearly every local family-restaurant table in the province.

items.name: Stir-fried Sataw with Fresh Shrimp
items.blurb: Stink beans stir-fried with shrimp paste and fresh prawns — pungent in the best possible way, the kind of heat-and-funk combination that works really well over steamed rice.

items.name: Gaeng Tai Pla
items.blurb: The South's most notorious curry — made from fermented fish entrails with vegetables, it is deeply funky, fiercely spicy, and a real litmus test for how much Southern heat you can handle.

items.name: Moo Hong
items.blurb: Hokkien-style pork belly braised slowly in soy sauce — sweet, salty, tender, and zero heat. A good starting point if you are still building up your Southern spice tolerance.

blocks.html: These picks come from review patterns and local word-of-mouth — spread across Takua Pa, Thai Mueang, and Phang Nga town itself. Always check opening hours before you go: local restaurants often close early or take a fixed day off each week.

items.name: Pa Da Hokkien Mee
items.blurb: A neighbourhood Hokkien mee shop in the Takua Pa old market. Noodles are sticky and well-cooked, finished with a runny egg and fresh veg on the side. This is the name that comes up first when people talk about Hokkien mee in Takua Pa.
items.meta: Takua Pa old market · Hokkien mee around ฿65

items.name: Ruea Khut Rae (Dredge Boat)
items.blurb: A restaurant and cafe in a palm grove along Phetkasem Road between Thai Mueang and Khao Lak. The signature is Mae Ngoi's Hokkien hor mok recipe, sold here since 1940 and made fresh daily. Available steamed, as a bao filling, or deep-fried.

items.name: Kai Tong (Dim Sum)
items.blurb: A morning dim sum shop in Takua Pa town, made fresh and served hot. One of the most popular breakfasts among locals in the area. Opens early and closes before noon.

items.name: Go Khun
items.blurb: A breakfast institution with over a hundred years of history in Takua Pa old town. Dim sum, you tiao (fried dough sticks), rice porridge, and drinks — classic kopitiam atmosphere throughout.

items.name: Jin Keng
items.blurb: A traditional kopitiam open for around 70 years in Takua Pa old town. Dim sum, bao, you tiao, and old-school brewed coffee — Hokkien breakfast the way it used to be.

items.name: Krua Aree Bang Mad
items.blurb: A local seafood restaurant in Bang Phat that gets regular mentions for value. Set meals run around ฿250/person with several dishes to share — relaxed atmosphere, works well for groups.

items.name: Tha Nun Seafood
items.blurb: A solid seafood spot near Koh Kloy, close to Sarasin Bridge before the crossing into Phuket. The tamarind shrimp — fried prawns in a sweet-sour sauce — is what people come here for.
items.meta: Koh Kloy, Takua Thung · near Sarasin Bridge

items.name: Je Nong Local Food
items.blurb: A proper Southern Thai restaurant in Phang Nga town that does not tone things down for tourists. Spice levels are what locals actually eat. Go here if you want the real thing, not the tourist-adjusted version.

blocks.title: Planning your meals
blocks.html: If you are passing through Phang Nga on the way to Khao Lak or Phang Nga Bay, put the Hokkien breakfast in Takua Pa first thing in the morning, then save dinner for seafood by the water. One day, two very different food experiences.

faq.q: What food is Phang Nga known for?
faq.a: Hokkien mee from Takua Pa is what most people point to first — thick yellow noodles stir-fried in a savoury sauce, topped with egg. Close behind are Hokkien hor mok, morning dim sum, fresh seafood from Phang Nga Bay, and Southern Thai staples like nam prik kung siab and stir-fried sataw with shrimp.

faq.q: Where is the best Hokkien mee in Phang Nga?
faq.a: The old market area of Takua Pa is the place. Pa Da Hokkien Mee is the name that comes up most often — noodles around ฿65 a plate. Most shops run breakfast through midday only, so plan to be there before noon.

faq.q: Is seafood expensive in Phang Nga?
faq.a: Generally cheaper than the bigger tourist destinations. Some restaurants around Bang Phat offer per-person set meals at around ฿250 with multiple dishes. Shrimp and crab prices vary with the season, so ask the price per kilogram and weight before you order.

faq.q: Where can I find Hokkien hor mok?
faq.a: Ruea Khut Rae (Dredge Boat) in Thai Mueang has been making it to Mae Ngoi's recipe since 1940 — steamed fresh daily. They also do it as a bao filling and deep-fried. Closed Tuesdays.

faq.q: How spicy is the Southern Thai food in Phang Nga?
faq.a: It can be very spicy — especially gaeng tai pla and the nam prik dishes. You can ask the kitchen to reduce the chilli, and most will. If you are still warming up to Southern spice, moo hong (braised pork belly) is a good entry point — no heat at all.
